lesson.title: No Two Electrons Alike: The Rule That Caps Every Orbital
lesson.summary: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in the same atom can have an identical set of four quantum numbers, which in practice means every orbital holds at most two electrons and those two must spin in opposite directions.
lesson.body:
Every electron in an atom can be described by a set of four quantum numbers: n (the shell), l (the subshell, or orbital shape), ml (which specific orbital within that subshell), and ms (the electron's spin, either plus one half or minus one half). Wolfgang Pauli's exclusion principle, formulated in 1925, makes a simple but powerful claim: no two electrons in the same atom can share all four quantum numbers at once. If two electrons happen to occupy the same orbital, meaning they already match on n, l, and ml, then the fourth quantum number, spin, must be different. That is the entire rule, and nearly everything you already know about electron configurations follows from it.

The most immediate consequence is the two electron limit per orbital that you have been using all along. An orbital is defined by a fixed n, l, and ml, so any two electrons sharing that same orbital have already matched three of the four quantum numbers. The only quantum number left to distinguish them is spin, and spin has only two possible values, so at most two electrons can occupy any single orbital, and they must have opposite spins, conventionally drawn as one arrow up and one arrow down. A third electron trying to enter that same orbital would need to duplicate all four quantum numbers of an electron already there, which the principle forbids outright.

This is exactly why subshell capacities work out the way they do. The s subshell has one orbital, so it holds at most 2 electrons. The p subshell has three orbitals, so it holds at most 6. The d subshell has five orbitals, so it holds at most 10. The f subshell has seven orbitals, so it holds at most 14. None of these numbers are arbitrary memorized facts; each one is simply two electrons per orbital, multiplied by however many orbitals that subshell contains, a direct arithmetic result of the Pauli exclusion principle combined with the orbital counts you learned earlier.

Helium offers the cleanest possible illustration. Its two electrons both occupy the 1s orbital, giving the configuration 1s2, and quantum mechanically this is only allowed because the two electrons have opposite spins, one ms = +1/2 and one ms = -1/2. If both electrons somehow had the same spin, they would have identical values for all four quantum numbers, which the Pauli exclusion principle strictly rules out; such a configuration simply does not exist in nature. This is not a subtle technicality: it is the reason helium's electron configuration has exactly two electrons in 1s and not three, and it is why lithium's third electron, atomic number 3, is forced into the higher energy 2s orbital rather than crowding into an already full 1s.

Beyond electron configurations, the Pauli exclusion principle has consequences that reach well past chemistry: it is the reason ordinary matter takes up space and does not collapse in on itself, since electrons cannot simply pile into the same lowest energy state. Within the scope of building electron configurations, though, its role is narrower and very concrete: it sets the hard ceiling of two electrons per orbital that every subshell capacity depends on, and it works hand in hand with Hund's rule to determine exactly how those electrons distribute themselves among degenerate orbitals before any pairing occurs.
